title: Improvement Exchange Planning
name: Improvement Exchange Planning
metaTitle: Improvement Exchange Planning in Phoenix, AZ
metaDescription: How build-to-suit improvement exchanges work for Phoenix investors using exchange funds to construct or renovate a replacement property before day 180.

sections.html:
An improvement exchange, sometimes called a build-to-suit exchange, lets an investor use exchange funds to construct or renovate a replacement property, with an accommodator holding title while the work gets done. The catch is that the construction clock runs inside the same 180-day exchange window as everything else, and Phoenix construction timelines do not always cooperate.

This structure gets used across the Phoenix metro more than investors expect, particularly where the available inventory of finished, move-in-ready buildings does not match what a specific tenant or buyer actually needs.

sections.heading: Why Investors Use an Accommodator to Build
sections.html:
Direct improvements cannot be made to a property the investor already owns and have them count toward the exchange, so an exchange accommodation titleholder holds title to the replacement property while improvements are completed with exchange funds. Once the work is done, or the 180-day period runs out, title transfers to the investor.

This structure exists because the tax code requires the investor to acquire replacement property, not simply improve property already owned. Routing the purchase and the construction through an accommodator is what keeps the improvements eligible as part of the exchange rather than a separate capital project.

sections.heading: The Construction Clock Runs Inside the Exchange Clock
sections.html:
This structure comes up most in the West Valley, where a Phoenix-area investor might be trading into a shell building near the Loop 303 corridor that needs dock doors, power upgrades, or racking improvements before it works for a supply-chain tenant. The improvements have to be substantially complete, and title has to transfer, before day 180. Construction delays that would be a minor headache on a normal build become an exchange-ending problem here.

A shell building that looks like a fast close on paper can turn into a tight finish once permitting and inspection schedules across the Phoenix metro get factored in.

The math has to work backward from day 180: if the accommodation titleholder needs two weeks to close and transfer title once construction is done, the actual building work has less than the full 180 days to finish, not the full period.

sections.heading: What Has to Actually Finish Before Day 180
sections.html:
Improvements identified on the 45-day list need to reflect the value they will have once completed, not the shell's current value, which means the appraisal work and construction scope need to be locked early:

  • Permits pulled and contractor bids finalized before the identification deadline
  • A draw schedule that matches how exchange funds are released
  • An accommodation titleholder agreement in place before construction starts
  • A completion appraisal ordered with enough lead time before day 180
  • A buffer built into the schedule for inspection delays

sections.heading: Where Improvement Exchanges Run Into Trouble in This Market
sections.html: Permitting and inspection timelines around West Valley industrial construction do not always match the pace investors expect from other parts of the country, and a single delayed inspection can push completion past day 180. Confirm realistic construction timelines with your contractor and accommodation titleholder before relying on an improvement exchange structure, and keep your tax advisor in the loop on how partially completed improvements are valued if the deadline is close.

sections.heading: Weighing an Improvement Exchange Against Buying Finished Product
sections.html:
A Phoenix investor deciding between a shell building near Loop 303 that needs work and a finished, stabilized building elsewhere in the West Valley is really weighing construction risk against a smaller inventory of ready-to-use options. Finished industrial product close to the semiconductor supply chain does not sit on the market long, which pushes some investors toward the improvement route even with the added timeline pressure.

Whichever path fits, the decision needs to be made early, since an improvement exchange leaves far less margin for delay than a straightforward purchase of a completed Phoenix building.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an improvement exchange and a regular exchange?
faqs.a: In an improvement exchange, exchange funds are used to construct or renovate the replacement property while an accommodation titleholder holds title, rather than simply purchasing a finished property outright.

faqs.q: Can I use exchange funds to improve a property I already own?
faqs.a: No. The property has to be held by an accommodation titleholder during the improvement period; funds cannot be used to improve real estate the investor directly owns.

faqs.q: What happens if construction is not finished by day 180?
faqs.a: Only the value of improvements actually completed and in place by day 180 counts toward the exchange. Anything unfinished at that point does not receive exchange treatment.

faqs.q: Do I need to identify the property before or after improvements are planned?
faqs.a: The property, including the planned scope of improvements, needs to be identified within the 45-day window, described specifically enough to reflect the improved value expected at completion.

faqs.q: Who holds title to the property during construction?
faqs.a: An exchange accommodation titleholder holds title while improvements are being completed with exchange funds. Title transfers to the investor once the work is done or the exchange period ends.

faqs.q: Can I use an improvement exchange for a renovation instead of new construction?
faqs.a: Yes. The same structure applies whether the work is ground-up construction or a substantial renovation of an existing Phoenix building, as long as the accommodation titleholder holds title during the improvement period and the work is completed inside the exchange window.

faqs.q: How much lead time should I build in for permitting on a Phoenix build-out?
faqs.a: Permitting timelines vary by jurisdiction and scope of work, so confirm specifics with the local building department and your contractor as early as possible, since a permitting delay is one of the more common threats to finishing before day 180.
